---
title: "Count overdispersion"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Poisson regression requires conditional mean and variance to be equal. **Overdispersion** occurs when the remaining variation is larger than that requirement permits. We diagnose it in the Nettle teaching model with [Pearson residuals](residuals.qmd) and use the [model-criticism logic](checking-linear-regression.qmd): a diagnostic identifies an assumption under strain, not a unique replacement model.

We first compute the diagnostic against the fitted Poisson means, then compare mechanisms that could produce the same excess variation.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-dispersion
#| echo: true
path <- "data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  nettle <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/",
                "applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(digest::digest(source_file, "sha256", file = TRUE, serialize = FALSE) ==
    "3c5abfbec7b2132a9b81ee9a178cbd5559426578032b60c6c4ad74046898793b")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file)
  nettle <- data.frame(country = raw$Country, log10_population = raw$Population,
    log10_area_km2 = raw$Area, log_area_km2 = log(10) * raw$Area,
    mean_growing_season_months = raw$MGS, language_count = as.integer(raw$Langs))
}
fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(log_area_km2),
           poisson(), nettle)
nettle$fitted <- fitted(fit)
nettle$pearson <- residuals(fit, type = "pearson")
dispersion <- sum(nettle$pearson^2) / df.residual(fit)
dispersion
```

The estimator is

$$

The numerator is the sum of squared standardized residuals because a Poisson row has model variance $\widehat\lambda_i$:

$$
r_i^P=\frac{y_i-\widehat\lambda_i}{\sqrt{\widehat\lambda_i}},
\qquad
\sum_i(r_i^P)^2=\sum_i\frac{(y_i-\widehat\lambda_i)^2}{\widehat\lambda_i}.
$$

The denominator $n-p$ accounts approximately for the $p$ fitted mean parameters. Under a correctly specified independent Poisson model, the numerator is approximately chi-squared with $n-p$ degrees of freedom, so the ratio fluctuates around one rather than equaling one exactly.
\widehat\phi=\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_i
\frac{(y_i-\widehat\lambda_i)^2}{\widehat\lambda_i}.
$$

A Poisson model expects a value near one. The observed value is `r round(dispersion, 2)`, so the conditional variance restriction fails badly for this specification.

```{r}
#| label: plot-nettle-dispersion
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nettle, aes(fitted, pearson)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#1F5A85") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Fitted language count", y = "Pearson residual") +
  theme_classic()
```

```{r}
#| label: observed-versus-fitted-count-variance
#| echo: true
nettle$fitted_bin <- cut(nettle$fitted,
  unique(quantile(nettle$fitted, seq(0, 1, length.out = 6))),
  include.lowest = TRUE)
variance_by_bin <- aggregate(cbind(language_count, fitted) ~ fitted_bin, nettle,
  function(z) c(mean = mean(z), variance = var(z), n = length(z)))
variance_by_bin
```

These bins are descriptive. A within-bin observed variance much larger than its fitted mean is compatible with overdispersion, but sparse bins and a changing mean can also produce gaps.

Overdispersion may arise from omitted heterogeneity, dependence, an inadequate mean formula, or a different count distribution. It is a diagnosis, not a mechanism.

| Possible source | Evidence to inspect | Corresponding next model |
|---|---|---|
| Mean formula too coarse | residual trend against climate or area | revise predictors or functional form |
| Unobserved unit heterogeneity | extra variance without a known cluster | negative-binomial mixture |
| Known clustered dependence | repeated observations within a group | random effects or clustered uncertainty |
| Mean plausible, variance scaled | coefficient estimates stable but SEs too small | quasi-Poisson uncertainty |
| More zeros than a single count process predicts | zero frequency and process knowledge | hurdle or zero-inflated model |

## Recap and check

1. Does $\widehat\phi=2$ prove a negative-binomial data-generating process? No. Several failures can inflate the same statistic.
2. Must a correct Poisson fit produce exactly one? No. The statistic has sampling variation around one.

The [quasi-Poisson page](quasi-poisson.qmd) changes uncertainty while retaining the fitted mean; the [negative-binomial page](negative-binomial-regression.qmd) changes the conditional variance model.
